title: Rethinking Data: Moving From the Traditional Three-Tier Web Stack to Client-Side Event Sourcing
gist: Prisma founder Johannes Schickling explains why he abandoned the traditional three-tier web stack for a client-side, event-sourced Local-First architecture (LiveStore), built to power his music app Overtone, and lays out a concrete framework for when event sourcing, CRDTs, or query-based sync engines each make sense.

insights.claim: Johannes Schickling founded Prisma to build server-side database tooling for the traditional three-tier web stack (database, API, client), but stepped away from it in 2020 to pursue a fundamentally different client-centric data architecture called Local-First.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: A well-known infra founder abandoning the architecture his own company was built on is a signal that three-tier/server-centric data stacks may be reaching a ceiling for UX-critical apps.
insights.locator: Rethinking Architecture for Superior User Experience

insights.claim: Schickling's frustration with database migrations at Prisma directly motivated his embrace of event sourcing, since it lets an application's data model evolve by replaying history through new logic rather than mutating a schema in place.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Migration pain is a recurring, underestimated cost center in data infrastructure; event-sourced designs are a direct response worth evaluating for teams facing the same problem.
insights.locator: Event Sourcing as a Foundational Technology

insights.claim: Schickling credits Ink and Switch's Local-First paper/essay as the pivotal influence that made him shift his entire focus away from server-centric tooling toward client-side data architectures starting in 2020.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Traces the intellectual lineage of the Local-First movement back to a single influential paper, useful for anyone mapping the space's origins and key voices (also including Martin Kleppmann and Adam Wiggins).
insights.locator: Rethinking Architecture for Superior User Experience

themes.theme: Local-First: What It Is and When It's Worth the Cost

insights.claim: Local-First is not simply offline support; it is a shift of the data bottleneck from the server to the client, aimed at unlocking desktop-grade responsiveness (instant reaction to clicks) in web and mobile apps.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Reframes 'offline-first' from a defensive feature into a core performance/UX strategy — relevant for any product team benchmarking against native-app responsiveness.
insights.quote: I know that data is always the bottleneck for a great user experience
insights.locator: Local-First: Bridging the Gap Between Desktop and Web

insights.claim: Local-First architecture is not a strict upgrade over cloud-centric design; it imposes real costs, especially in upfront data-model planning and in reasoning about unbounded data growth on the client, so it should only be adopted when the UX payoff (offline capability, data ownership) clearly justifies the complexity.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Gives architects a cost/benefit gate rather than treating Local-First as a fashionable default — useful for scoping build-vs-avoid decisions.
insights.locator: When to Adopt Local-First Architectures

insights.claim: Schickling's decision framework for adopting Local-First reduces to two questions: how important is it that the app works offline or under poor connectivity, and how important is it for end users to own their data — only pursue Local-First when the answers are strongly 'yes.'
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Actionable go/no-go checklist product and engineering leads can apply before committing to a Local-First rewrite.
insights.quote: how important is it that your application works offline is one
insights.locator: When to Adopt Local-First Architectures

insights.claim: Applications that decompose cleanly into self-contained units — such as a single Linear issue or a single Figma canvas/workspace — are good Local-First candidates; applications shaped like a social network, where everything is interconnected with everything, are a sign Local-First is the wrong fit.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: A concrete architectural litmus test: if your data can't be sliced into small independent boundaries, don't force a Local-First rewrite.
insights.quote: If you built rather something that feels like a social network where you can't really draw that boundary where everything is connected with everything, this is a sign that you don't have a good use case for a Local-First at your hand.
insights.locator: When to Adopt Local-First Architectures

insights.claim: For domains where correctness dominates over client responsiveness, such as a global financial system, a 1-2 second loading spinner is an acceptable trade-off to avoid race-condition errors, and Local-First is the wrong architecture there.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Useful counter-example for fintech/critical-systems teams tempted to chase Local-First hype: prioritize server-side consistency guarantees over local speed when money/safety is at stake.
insights.quote: let's say you're building a global financial system, it's much more important that there's never a mistake happening where someone losing a million dollars because of some race condition
insights.locator: Event Sourcing vs CRDTs

insights.claim: Schickling recommends time-boxing a first Local-First prototype (e.g., building with Automerge), checking whether a blocking issue emerges, and being willing to walk away and conclude the architecture 'was not worth it' rather than over-analyzing indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Practical de-risking tactic: cap exploration cost before fully committing engineering resources to a Local-First migration.
insights.locator: When to Adopt Local-First Architectures

insights.claim: Event sourcing and CRDTs solve the same underlying distributed-systems consistency problem, just exposed differently: event sourcing preserves a full replayable history, while CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types) make mutable objects, arrays, or sets auto-merge without conflict across machines.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Core mental model for architects choosing a Local-First sync strategy: pick based on whether you need causal history or just convergent state.
insights.locator: Event Sourcing vs CRDTs

insights.claim: Schickling deliberately avoided a pure CRDT approach for LiveStore because mutable data is 'the source of all evil' — it makes it hard to trace where a change came from — and instead built an event-sourced model where application logic can be changed and the entire event history replayed.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: A named technical bet against the more popular CRDT camp (Automerge/Yjs), explaining why some architects choose event sourcing for auditability over CRDTs' convenience.
insights.quote: mutable data is sort of typically the source of all evil
insights.locator: Event Sourcing vs CRDTs

insights.claim: As a rule of thumb, simple data types — a number needing only plus/minus, or an add/remove set like GitHub labels — are well served by CRDTs/Automerge; event sourcing pays off more when the full causal history of changes matters.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Gives a quick heuristic to route a given feature's data model to CRDTs vs event sourcing rather than treating the choice as all-or-nothing per app.
insights.locator: Event Sourcing vs CRDTs

insights.claim: Martin Kleppmann's 'turning the database inside out' talk is the conceptual root of the event-sourcing path Schickling took, framing event sourcing as exposing a database's internal change log as the primary interface.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Points investors/architects to the specific conceptual source underpinning a growing class of event-sourced Local-First tools.
insights.quote: Martin has given a great talk at some point about turning the database inside out, which is what is event sourcing.
insights.locator: Local-First: Bridging the Gap Between Desktop and Web

insights.claim: Beyond CRDTs and event sourcing, a third Local-First/sync approach keeps an authoritative centralized database (closer to a traditional Rails-style stack) and streams query-defined subsets to the client as an always-up-to-date smart cache; this is the model used by Zero, ElectricSQL, and PowerSync.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Maps a third competitive lane in the sync-engine market distinct from CRDT (Automerge/Yjs/Loro) and event-sourcing (LiveStore) camps — relevant for tracking which vendors serve which architecture pattern.
insights.locator: Local-First as a Radical Shift in Data Philosophy

themes.theme: LiveStore and Overtone: Architecture in Practice

insights.claim: LiveStore originated as a research project called Riffle that Schickling built with Nicholas Schiefer and Geoffrey Litt, both MIT PhDs at the time, exploring a SQLite-based, event-sourcing Local-First framework.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Names the specific research lineage and people behind LiveStore, useful for due diligence on the technology's origins and credibility.
insights.quote: I also teamed up with Nicholas Schiefer and Geoffrey Litt on a research project back then called Riffle
insights.locator: Event Sourcing as a Foundational Technology

insights.claim: LiveStore's core technical innovation is pairing a reactive, in-thread SQLite database (fast enough to run alongside the front-end web app) with an event-sourcing-based sync engine.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific engineering combination (reactive local SQLite + event-sourced sync) that differentiates LiveStore from CRDT-based competitors like Automerge.
insights.locator: LiveStore - An SQLite With Sync Engine Capabilities

insights.claim: LiveStore's sync model mirrors Git's push-pull workflow: local changes generate events that get pushed to a sync server, and if the server already has newer state, the client must pull/rebase before pushing again.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Gives engineers a familiar mental model (Git semantics) for reasoning about conflict handling in an event-sourced Local-First sync engine.
insights.quote: The way how it works is very similar to how Git works.
insights.locator: Event Sourcing vs CRDTs

insights.claim: In LiveStore's architecture the client, not the server, holds the source of truth; the sync backend exists only to propagate and back up data across a user's devices and enable real-time collaboration.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: A clear architectural inversion versus the traditional server-authoritative model — key for evaluating data-durability and offline guarantees of LiveStore-based apps.
insights.quote: all of the data that actually has the source of truth in LiveStore, the source of truth has been the client
insights.locator: LiveStore - An SQLite With Sync Engine Capabilities

insights.claim: LiveStore is open source but, as of this interview, still not fully production-ready, though a community is forming around it.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Sets current maturity expectations for teams evaluating LiveStore for production adoption versus experimentation.
insights.locator: Event Sourcing as a Foundational Technology

insights.claim: Overtone is Schickling's Local-First music curation app, acting as a third-party client layer over wherever a user's music actually lives (Spotify, purchased files, etc.), analogous to how Superhuman functions as a third-party client for a Gmail account.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Frames a reusable product pattern — the 'third-party client layer' — for building better UX on top of commoditized backend services you don't control.
insights.quote: it's sort of like a third-party client for wherever music lives in the same way as how you can use Superhuman, for example, with your Gmail account
insights.locator: Event Sourcing as a Foundational Technology

insights.claim: Overtone deliberately does not try to own or reinvent music storage or streaming; its entire innovation budget goes into a rich metadata and tagging layer defined by the end user rather than the app's developer.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Shows a disciplined scoping choice — competing on a thin, defensible metadata layer instead of costly infrastructure (streaming rights, storage) that incumbents already own.
insights.locator: LiveStore - An SQLite With Sync Engine Capabilities

insights.claim: Overtone handles volatile external data — e.g., Spotify removing a track from its catalog — by keeping a 'tombstone' record that preserves the user's tags and metadata, and de-duplicates automatically if the same track later appears from another source.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: A concrete, reusable data-integrity pattern for any app that aggregates and enriches records from unreliable third-party sources.
insights.quote: I still want to have sort of like a tombstone of a track where all the tags that I've added is still there
insights.locator: LiveStore - An SQLite With Sync Engine Capabilities

insights.claim: Schickling describes preventing data loss or corruption in Overtone as his 'highest-order bid,' on top of making the app feel as fast and responsive as a triple-A video game.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Signals that for Local-First consumer apps, data durability is treated as a harder constraint than raw performance — a priority ordering other builders can adopt.
insights.quote: This was for me, the highest-order bid basically, additionally to unlocking the best possible user experience where the app feels as fast as like a triple A game.
insights.locator: LiveStore - An SQLite With Sync Engine Capabilities

insights.claim: Schickling treats rigorous schema design as the critical mechanism for both ingesting messy, differently-formatted external data (e.g., Spotify's format vs. Amazon Music's format) and for guaranteeing future data interoperability and exportability.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Positions schema rigor as a durable moat for data portability, and notes it is becoming even more important as AI tools consume and reshape structured data.
insights.quote: my answer is always great schemas
insights.locator: Data Ownership and Interoperability

insights.claim: Overtone/LiveStore users can access both the raw source-of-truth event log (a sequence of JSON blobs) and a materialized SQLite database, giving them full data portability to leave the app or feed the data into another tool or an AI assistant like Claude.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that event-sourced Local-First design can deliver genuine data-export/ownership guarantees, not just marketing claims — a differentiator versus closed SaaS platforms.
insights.locator: Data Ownership and Interoperability

insights.claim: GDPR's mandated data-export requirement, despite not enforcing a single standard format, has been an underappreciated step forward for data interoperability because it forces services to provide some complete export that can bootstrap a new Local-First app.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Reframes a compliance regulation as unintentional infrastructure for the Local-First and data-portability movement — relevant to policy watchers and builders relying on export rights.
insights.quote: with the advent of GDPR, we actually got a really huge step forward in terms of data interoperability
insights.locator: Data Ownership and Interoperability

insights.claim: Schickling points to Google Docs, Figma, and Linear as proof points that a fundamentally different client-side data architecture (enabling live cursors and real-time collaboration in the browser) represents a genuine step-function UX improvement over traditional web apps — Linear specifically outperforms Jira and GitHub Issues on this dimension.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Sets the UX bar Overtone (and other Local-First apps) is being benchmarked against, and highlights which incumbent products are vulnerable to being out-executed on responsiveness/collaboration.
insights.locator: Local-First: Bridging the Gap Between Desktop and Web

insights.claim: The localfirst.fm podcast initiative produced a 'Local-First landscape' comparison mapping competing technologies (Automerge, Yjs, Loro, ElectricSQL, PowerSync, LiveStore, and others) across multiple dimensions for architects evaluating options.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: A ready-made competitive map of the Local-First tooling market for anyone doing vendor/technology selection in this space.
insights.locator: Event Sourcing as a Foundational Technology

insights.claim: Schickling co-organizes the Local-First conference in Berlin, featuring speakers Martin Kleppmann and Adam Wiggins, spanning two conference days plus a third hands-on hacking day.
insights.speaker: Johannes Schickling
insights.so_what: Identifies a concrete industry gathering point for tracking Local-First adoption momentum and who the leading voices are.
insights.locator: Data Ownership and Interoperability
